passage:
In the girls' hostel of the boarding school in Shillong, Maria found out at dinner that Nandini had told the whole dorm about her crush. Back in her room, face burning, she typed fast into the class group: 'Nandini can't keep one secret. Don't tell her anything.' Three friends reacted with laughing faces within seconds. For a moment it felt great.
By lights-out, Nandini was crying in the bathroom, and Maria's stomach had turned to stone. She deleted the message, but twenty-eight people had already seen it.
Next morning the counsellor, Ms Kharkongor, listened to both girls. Afterwards she said to Maria, 'Angry messages feel urgent. Try this rule: type it, don't send it, sleep on it.'
Maria wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it to her phone cover.

qa.q: How many people had already seen Maria's message before it was deleted?
qa.a: Twenty-eight people had already seen it.

qa.q: What did Maria feel by lights-out, and what caused the change?
qa.a: Maria felt heavy regret, her stomach like stone, after hearing Nandini crying in the bathroom.

qa.q: What choice did Maria make after the counsellor's advice?
qa.a: She wrote the rule 'type it, don't send it, sleep on it' on a sticky note and stuck it to her phone cover.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt seeing the message in the class group?
qa.a: Nandini likely felt humiliated and hurt at being called out in front of the class, even if sharing the secret was wrong.

grounding: Shows a teenager sending an angry message in the heat of the moment, regretting it, and adopting a sleep-on-it rule.

passage:
Dear Anand bhaiya,
Remember the birthday money Nani gave me, the money I was saving for the art course? It's gone. On Saturday at the mall, my friends kept saying how cool the glowing headphones were, a sale was ending in ten minutes, my heart was pounding, and I just paid. All of it.
For one evening I felt amazing. By Sunday I felt sick. They're just headphones. The art course starts next month.
You always say you wait a night before any big buy. I used to think that was boring. Now I get it: when I'm excited and everyone's watching, my brain doesn't look past the next ten minutes.
So I'm making it my rule too. Anything that costs more than I spend in a week, I sleep on first.
I'm going to tell Nani myself this weekend.
Damini

qa.q: What was the birthday money from Nani meant for?
qa.a: The art course.

qa.q: Why did Damini pay for the headphones so quickly?
qa.a: Excitement, friends calling the headphones cool and a sale ending in ten minutes made Damini's heart pound, so Damini acted without looking past the moment.

qa.q: What rule does Damini choose now, and why might it help?
qa.a: Sleeping on anything that costs more than a week's spending gives the excitement time to cool, so Damini can see past the next ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Anand bhaiya feel reading that the 'boring' habit now makes sense to Damini?
qa.a: Anand bhaiya might feel pleased and a little amused, and glad Damini is owning the mistake and planning to tell Nani.

grounding: Shows a teenager making a rash purchase under excitement and peer pressure, regretting it, and adopting a sleep-on-it rule.

passage: Beatriz saw the photo at 11 p.m.: Ines and the others on the beach at Cascais, a trip nobody had told her about. Her face burned. Her older brother, over breakfast, said, "Rule I learned the hard way: anything written after ten at night waits till morning." Beatriz typed a new message to Ines, slowly: "I'm sorry. I felt left out and I exploded." She saved the rule as her phone's lock screen.

passage:
Dear Shankar-mama,
Thank you for the birthday money. I have to tell you what I did with it, because hiding it feels worse. On the night of my birthday my friends were all buying outfits in an online game, and everyone in the voice chat was saying, "Just buy it, Trisha, it's only once." In twenty minutes I had spent all of it. Every rupee. The next morning I felt sick. Amma was disappointed, but she didn't shout; she helped me write to the game company asking for a refund, and we're waiting. I've made a rule for myself: if I want to buy something, I wait one full night and ask Amma first. I'm sorry. I wanted you to hear it from me.
Trisha

qa.q: How long did it take Trisha to spend the money?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel the morning after spending the money?
qa.a: Trisha felt sick with regret and guilt.

qa.q: What rule did Trisha make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Waiting a full night and asking Amma first, so peer pressure and excitement cool before buying.

qa.q: How might Shankar-mama feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Shankar-mama may feel disappointed about the money but touched by Trisha's honesty.

grounding: Shows a teen who makes a rash purchase under peer pressure, regrets it and adopts a wait-a-night rule with a trusted adult.

passage:
Gargi, don't laugh, okay? It's me, Jahnavi, and this week I did two really dumb things.
First, Tanya said something mean about my dance video in the class group. I was so angry my hands were shaking, and I typed this huge paragraph back, full of stuff about her family, and sent it. Everyone saw. The next morning I read it again and felt sick. That wasn't even me.
Then on Saturday, the mall had a sale, all my friends were buying, and I spent my whole birthday money on sneakers I didn't even like. Everyone said, "Buy it!" and I just did.
Both times I felt this rush, like I had to do it right now. Both times I regretted it by morning.
So I've made myself a rule: if I'm angry or everyone's pushing, I sleep on it. Tanya's apology message is sitting in my drafts right now. I'm sending it tomorrow, after I've slept.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi buy with the birthday money?
qa.a: Sneakers Jahnavi didn't even like.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel the morning after the angry message?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt sick with regret and ashamed, feeling the message wasn't even the real Jahnavi.

qa.q: Why is "sleep on it" a protective rule for Jahnavi?
qa.a: Strong anger and friends pushing gave Jahnavi a rush to act right away; waiting until morning lets the emotion settle so foresight can return.

qa.q: How might Tanya feel when she reads Jahnavi's apology?
qa.a: Tanya may feel relieved and respected after the hurtful message about her family, though she may also see her own mean comment differently.

grounding: Shows a teen who sends an angry message and makes a rash purchase under strong emotion and peer pressure, then adopts a sleep-on-it rule.
